She is also the author of Taking Down the Lion, which is the center of attention for this episode. The book explores the fall of Tyco International's CEO and Chairman, Dennis Kozlowski, who was convicted of stealing more than 100 million dollars from the company. For more info about the podcast, go to the episode page and make sure to follow us on Twitter . transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye.
I'm your host, Eri Parmion, and with me here in the studio is my friend and colleague, Niklas
Savos.
How are you?
I'm great.
I've really been looking forward to our upcoming interview since I love to read about
corporate scandals and I was not disappointed by reading this book.
Neither was I.
In today's episode of Investing by the Books, we have the great pleasure of speaking to
Katherine Esnil.
Kathy has worked as an attorney and is since 2005 an associate professor of Business Ethics
and Business Law at Northern Kentucky University.
She's also the author of Taking Down the Lion, which we will discuss today.
What is the book about?
The book covers the story of the big American conglomerate, Tyco International, and its
long-time CEO, Dennis Koslovsky.
In 2001, revenues amounted to 36 billion dollars, and Business Week ranked Tyco the number
one performing company in the S&P 500.
Koslovsky worked at Tyco for 27 years and held the helm of the company for about 10 years.
And as CEO and Chairman, he did hundreds of acquisitions and was greatly admired until
he suddenly lost his job in 2002.
Ultimately, he was convicted of grand larceny and other crimes that found him guilty of wrongfully
taking 100 million from Tyco.
This is indeed a fascinating story with crucial lessons for both operators and investors.
So how does the book fit with the quality rating here at Radoi?
So this book centers on the people aspects of a business, and as we will discuss, a company
needs a competent management team, but also a strong board, and Tyco arguably lacked a
letter according to the author.
The company also tried to grow by making larger and larger acquisitions, and having my
serial acquirer had on, that strategy seldom works.
Professor Neil was granted unprecedented access to Dennis Koslovsky, his papers, family,
friends, attorneys, and former Tyco colleagues, as well as transcripts and evidence from
two criminal trials.
Taking down the line was first published by Macmillan in 2014, and we are grateful to have
his author on the show today.
Here comes our conversation with Catherine S. Neil.
So hello, Kathy, and welcome to investing by the book's podcast.
Hi, thanks for having me.
It's great to have you on.
Where are you today?
I am in Highland Heights, Kentucky, which is a small college town just across the Ohio
river from Cincinnati, Ohio.
So I can see downtown Cincinnati from our business here.
Our business building on campus here.
And to begin, can you tell our listeners about your background and what led you into the
world of business ethics and business law?
Sure, Ken.
I am an attorney by profession.
I also have an undergraduate degree in business prior to going to law school.
I worked in business at Procter and Gamble, I'm sure you're familiar with, which is the
global headquarters of Procter and Gamble are here in Cincinnati.
Worked there prior to going to law school, went to law school, practice business, and corporate, and tax law, and a firm in downtown Cincinnati.
And then I completely changed my life and went into academia.
I did that, gosh, 20, 20 years ago.
So I've been, I was at the University of Cincinnati for a few years, and then I've been at Northern Kentucky University in the
Ohio College of Business since 2005, so getting to be a long time ago, you know.
And you're the author of the book, Taking Down the Lion that we will discuss today.
So in your own words, can you briefly introduce us to the story?
Sure.
This is the only book as far as I know that has ever been published about
the Taiko International Corporate Scandal that rolled out in 2002.
This is a case that received a lot of media attention.
I started teaching business ethics in 2005, the fall of 2005 here at NKU.
And even in that first semester that I taught that class, I use a lot of case studies in there just as, you know, it's just a great way for students to really critically think about the decisions that are made ethical decisions that are made in business.
And I've talked about the Taiko case since that fall of 2005, and that was actually the fall that Dennis Coslowski, who was the CEO, who was wrapped up in this scandal along with the CFO of Taiko, they were sentenced in September of 2005.
So I've been talking about it since the beginning.
The odd thing about this case was, and what drew my interest, is that there are many differences in this case from the other huge corporate scandals that happened in the United States about that same time.
The Enron bankruptcy, World Com, bankruptcy, you know, there was a long list of scandals, Martha Stewart,
the health south, but there was something about the Taiko case, even as I talked about it in class with my students that I never felt I fully understood.
I would try to explain it, and I heard myself every semester saying, I'm not really exactly sure what happened here, because there are some big differences than the other big scandals.
And the other thing was that Taiko never declared bankruptcy, they were financially sound throughout the scandal, and after the crimes that were charged among the corporate leaders at Taiko were not crimes that were investigated and prosecuted by the United States government, which is the norm.
For these big scandals that would have been the SEC investigation or US attorneys, in this case, that all of the criminal charges were brought by a local district attorney, which is highly unusual in a white collar financial crime case of this size or of any size.
So, you know, that was a bit difficult for me to understand.
And then looking at so many of these financial scandals involve financial statements that are wildly misleading to anyone who would use them for information.
But in this case that wasn't true, there was never any material restatements of the financial statements after the scandal broke.
So, it was those differences that really kind of drew me into the case, mostly because I didn't understand at all what was happening.
You know, like I would try to explain it to my students so that they could understand so that we could all learn something from the case, but it was very confusing to me.
And we will get deep into the details.
But first, to put things a bit in perspective, how big was Taiko at its peak and can you compare the company in terms of size and influence to a company today?
I can. You know, when Dennis Koslowski started working at Taiko, he started there in 1971 and it was a relatively small company based in New Hampshire, with annual revenue of about $20 million.
By 2001, which was the last year before the scandal, their annual revenue was $40 billion.
They were at that time one of the 50 largest companies in the world by market cap, I think, and annual revenue.
They were making $150 million a day in sales.
So they were quite substantial. If I think about companies now, I've been adjusting for the 20 years since this happened.
You know, this would be on the level size wise of annual revenue of a company like PNG or Intel or MetLife, even Walt Disney.
You know, so really large companies, interestingly, though, Taiko has never really been a household name, even even at its peak.
I don't think that most people knew Taiko, like all of the other big companies at that time, Taiko was a conglomerate of a lot of really.
Not glamorous businesses, you know, there wasn't anything very specifically interesting to most people, pipes and valves, electronics, medical devices, things like that.
The big brand that most people would have heard of was ADT security, which in the United States is a common lots of the homes and businesses have ADT security signs on their property.
That's a well known brand here and Taiko acquired ADT security at one point, but for the most part, most people did not know the name of Taiko very well.
In the book, you compare them at some points with the general electric.
Yes, not just me, there were many people at the time who were watching what Taiko was doing and thought that they were modeling the company after GE, the types of acquisitions that they made, the types of businesses that they became interested in.
So yeah, that was that was a common comparison at the time.
And as mentioned, Dennis Koslovsky is the lion in the book title and the main character of the story. Can you tell us a bit more about him?
I can. He is an incredibly interesting person, as you might imagine, someone who reaches the heights in his career that he did and then the lows as well.
He grew up very modestly in New Jersey, probably what would be considered a lower middle class family did not come from wealth, started working at a very young age and worked all through school, all through paid his, paid his own way through college.
And everyone I talk to about him always described him as the hardest working person they knew. So he's a very hard working, ambitious, very smart person who once he got into his career at Taiko was known for an aggressive growth mentality.
He really just focused on growing the company. And that took him from what he started at Taiko as an internal auditor, so a low level position.
And through his, his own work and success in the company, progressed all the way to CEO.
We'll talk more about him and what we can learn from how he acted in the company. But we're also curious to know a bit more about how it was when you wrote the book. Why did you do it and how was it to write it?
Well, I, as I mentioned earlier, I was just confused and curious about what really happened in this scandal. And in looking back, what was it completely random act on my part? And I'm sure I was sitting in my office.
I'm sure I had a long list of work to do. But instead of doing the work, I was thinking about this case and wondering how I could better understand it, where I could get more information. And I thought, well, Dennis Coslowski, he would know, you know, he would know the most.
And I knew he was still in prison at that time. This was in 2011, so 12 years ago, about this time of year.
So I looked online to see where he, which prison he was housed in in New York State and got an address. And I wrote a brief letter explaining who I was and asking if he would be willing to answer some questions for me just so I could better understand the case, the company, his role so that I could explain it in my classes.
So I sent this letter and honestly didn't think much else about it. I didn't invest much time in it and send it out. And a few weeks later, I walked into my department office and the administrative assistant said, hey, you've got a letter from a prison in your mailbox.
And it was a handwritten one page letter from him saying he would be happy to answer any questions that I had about the company and that he would have to do it just through handwritten letters because that's all we had access to in prison.
And so that started a series of me writing sending him questions and him sending handwritten responses to me.
I was just answering my questions about what happened. Of course, that was a lot for him to have to write out a whole history of the company with just to handwrite it.
So at some point months into that and it was a lengthy process as correspondence goes in and out of a prison, it takes a long time because they read everything going in and they read everything going out and you know, so it was a lengthy process.
So months into this he suggested that if I would be willing to travel, we could cover a lot more ground if we met in person.
So, of course, you know, in my position as a professor, it's just a really rare opportunity when you would get to meet someone that you've talked about in class for years and have access to them.
So I said, yes, of course, and even though I'm an attorney, I have never been anywhere near a jail or a prison of any time.
So it was that the experience of going into a maximum security prison was was something.
And so I did go and I was able to meet with him on visitors days, which I believe were 8 am to 3 pm where I would we would just sit at a table in a visitor's room.
And I could ask him questions and he would answer my questions.
The difficult part of that arrangement was I wasn't allowed to take in any notes or pen or paper or anything to write anything down.
So I had to try to remember, you know, and you could imagine seven hours of uninterrupted conversation, you can cover a lot of material.
So as soon as I would get to my car, I had a little digital recorder and I would try to recall everything that we talked about for seven hours.
But I then started really understanding the case and as it rolled out, it was just so very different than everything I had ever read about the case.
Even things that are in textbooks in the field of business ethics, the information in those textbooks was just completely different than the things he was telling me.
So those conversations, ultimately it was Dennis who suggested or asked if I might be interested in writing a book because he had been approached by people prior to me talking to him about about a book.
He had become distrustful. Most of those people, maybe all of them were from the media journalists of some type.
And he had become very distrustful of journalists if you've read any of the coverage of him in the case you could understand why he might not be interested in a journalist or cooperating with a journalist to write this story.
So we talked about that and I said, yeah, I might be interested. My whole objective with the book was for it to be accurate.
That was the whole point for me was to produce the accurate telling of what happened in this scandal.
I was fortunate that he did give me access to his attorneys and he had a lot of attorneys over those years who had corporate documents from those years.
And when I say corporate documents, I mean tens of thousands of corporate documents.
And the transcripts and evidence from two lengthy criminal trials.
So those were things that, you know, not to say that I distrusted what he was telling me that of course I wanted to be able to have other sources of information as they put the book together.
It was incredibly helpful but also incredibly time consuming to sift through thousands of corporate documents to make sure so I can see what really happened.
But that's where the story got really interesting for me because I could read reporting in what I had always considered to be highly reliable, respected sources.
And then I would be looking at documents and evidence and a trial that completely contradict the things in those articles and that was, you know, unexpected for me.
It must have been a very special situation being this business ethics professor and even in law and then on the other hand have such a close contact with him, the convicted person.
It was an interesting opportunity to talk about someone, you know, all of us who do what I do, you know, you talk about different people in classes but you don't really know those people, you know, you don't really ever get a chance to interact with those people.
So it was a great opportunity for me and then ultimately my students who get kind of a firsthand view also.
But it must be easy to get emotionally in this kind of and very engaged in this kind of story I can imagine.
How did you stay objective besides reading all those documents?
Well, yeah, that was the, you know, fortunately, he never pressured me to twist the story or to, you know, in fact, he never saw anything that was written until it had already gone to the publisher.
So he didn't have any, any influence over what I wrote or how I wrote it or how I my opinion about it.
As I said, my main goal was to be accurate.
That was, you know, and that, you know, I know looking at the book, even now as I go back and look at it, you know, I write like a lawyer, I write like an attorney, I footnote everything, I, you know, I was incredibly conscientious about being accurate.
I know he's very controversial, I know that if it was, if I, if I didn't have sources for what I included in the book that it would be criticized or even criticized by myself.
So, you know, I really never felt that really wasn't too difficult because again, my goal throughout was to be accurate.
You know, my editor, she kept, you know, so you don't want all these footnotes and it's like, but I do, I do, I do want all the footnotes because that's what I'm doing.
I'm telling this story from the facts, from the sources, the documents that exist, you know, so that's why there, you know, there are hundreds and hundreds of footnotes in the book at the back of the book.
I mean, if I found it really interesting to read about all the events, I mean, from, from Dennis Koslovsky and Mark Swartz, the CFO, being convicted of this crime and about, I mean, why they were convicted, maybe you can give us some more background on that.
What actually happened and, I mean, how, how are the proceedings with them getting sentenced and how long were they imprisoned and so on?
Most significant crimes that they were charged with were grand larceny that was stealing from the company.
And that theft with the prosecutors, that was in the form of four very large bonuses.
And here's what's interesting.
Those bonuses were paid based on a written pay for performance compensation plan.
You know, it wasn't just some numbers that were pulled out of the air, there was a written compensation plan, which by the way was in place prior to Dennis Koslovsky becoming CEO.
So it's not a compensation policy that he came up with or suggested or it was already there.
The big difference was the company had grown so significantly.
So what used to be relatively small bonuses based on the mathematical calculation included in that compensation plan, you know, you start adding several zeros after those numbers.
And those become what many people, including myself, would consider ridiculously large bonuses.
You know, I mean, and that's, you know, one of my biggest criticisms here was a lack of oversight by everyone.
I mean, you know, at some point that policy should have been reviewed to see if it still made sense for the company, you know, is that reasonable is that, you know, but it just never was.
So there are these four huge bonuses based on the profitability of four huge transactions.
And it wasn't just Koslovsky and Swartz who got bonuses, there were other people involved in those transactions who received bonuses at the same time.
Of course, they weren't as large as Koslovsky and Swartz bonuses, but so they got these four big bonuses.
The problem was there was no clear record keeping in whether the board knew about the bonuses, when they knew about the bonuses, were the bonuses paid at the right time.
You know, it was done, they were done in a undocumented manner, even though, and I check this myself, the mathematical calculation of the amounts was correct, according to the compensation policy.
But the questions then started coming up, well, did they get them too early or did the board, there were two criminal trials for Koslovsky and Swartz were tried together.
The first criminal trial lasted six months.
It was declared a mistrial while the jury was deliberating.
So there was a second trial that lasted five months, and it was at the conclusion of that trial that they were both convicted.
During those trials, some of the directors from Tyco testified that either they didn't remember, didn't recall if they knew about those bonus payments or that they testified that they weren't told about them.
Now, you know, there is even a question in my mind, there was nothing in the compensation policy that required board approval before those payments were made.
I don't, you know, so I'm not even sure why the focus was kind of on whether the board approved them, because if they had not paid them, then they're in violation of, you know, their own, their own compensation policies.
Okay, so they paid the bonuses, but Tyco, not unlike other large corporations like a GE or other corporations at the time, used to regularly loan money to their key executives, key employees, they'd have loan programs and Tyco did had a couple of loan programs.
Tyco had a, what was called a key employee loan program where they would loan again, huge amounts of money to key employees to prevent them from selling Tyco stock that was, that was vested when, when taxes were due on that stock, you know, so they wanted to encourage these key folks to hang on to their Tyco stock.
They wanted them selling the stock to take care of the tax bill, they'd say, don't do that. We'll loan you $20 million instead and you can pay your taxes.
You know, so all of these including Coslowski and Swartz have these huge loans due to Tyco.
For the bonuses, some of them weren't paid just as, you know, a cash bonus to Coslowski or Swartz, they were used to pay off the loan that they owed the company.
Mistakenly, they often refer to this as loan forgiveness, wasn't really forgiveness because they earned the bonus and then they used it to pay off the loan, but they called it loan forgiveness.
And when that starts getting reported, it's reported as, well, they're just, they're borrowing money and then the company's forgiving it, you know, and these were huge, $25 million, $30 million.
You know, so it was a lot of money flying around and it was done haphazardly, you know, that that was the, you know, if I had to point to the number one problem, it was for a huge corporation, they ran it like a mom and pop shop.
Very informally, didn't recognize corporate formalities, didn't keep good records, which, you know, ended up coming back to hurt, you know, several of those people very much.
Charlie Munger, one of our idols has said that the world is not driven by greed, but by envy, and I think you describe one incident in that, though where the company paid one of the board members, a large fee for having helped matchmaking a large acquisition, and the other board members got upset driven by this envy, so can you please tell us this story?
Yes, you know, we spoke earlier about how it looked like Tyco was modeling itself after a GE, and one thing that GE had at the time was GE Capital, so they had their own financial arm of the company, so Tyco decided they wanted to acquire a financial arm as well.
So they did and that the initial conversations between that company and Tyco were facilitated by one of the Tyco board members, you know, and quite honestly, it wasn't, it wasn't like he invested a lot of time or work, but it was his relationships that facilitated that acquisition ultimately.
Kuzlowski agreed to give him a 20 million dollar binder speed. Now, would you go back and look, and this is a big problem, almost every member of the board of directors of Tyco, over those years, had some type of additional relationship with the company.
They were leasing jets to the company, they were buying assets or selling assets to the company, so this certainly wasn't the only board member who was receiving additional compensation over and above board fees, but it was the amount and you're exactly right.
It wasn't that they thought that was wrong, it was, where's mine, you know, like why is he getting 20 million dollars, and where's my 20 million dollars.
So you're right, that's exactly what it was, and that set off this huge string of events, you know, the anger, well, you know, the company had run very smoothly for 10 years.
Kuzlowski was CEO for 10 years, everyone was happy, investors were happy, employees were happy, the board was happy, you know, so the longer that everyone was pleased with the performance, the less hands on everyone was the board just gave Kuzlowski freedom to do whatever he wanted with little or no oversight.
So making money is from their board fees, but more importantly, from the other relationships they have with the company.
Then in 2001, there was a recession in the United States, so it was the first time really that they, you know, they had benefited from the boom market of the 90s, so, you know, it was the first time that the stock price dropped a little.
Then we had the terrorist attacks in September of 2001, in the market crashed.
And that was the first time that the board started questioning Kuzlowski at all started expressing any unhappiness, and then this big finders fees to one of the directors really set them off.
They were already getting pressure and feeling unhappy, and then when they found out about that, then it set off this whole thing.
Then this is just a series of unfortunate events if you look at it from Kuzlowski's perspective.
Then in June of 2002, so this is following up, they're already unhappy with the $20 million payment, they're trying to get him to pay it back.
He's refusing to pay it back.
Kuzlowski is charged with sales tax evasion, completely unrelated to Tyco.
This is a personal purchase of art through a, through a art dealer, and there just happened to be at that time in Manhattan and New York City.
The district attorney was cracking down on individuals, wealthy individuals who were buying expensive things outside of the city and transporting them into the city.
Those things are subject to an 8% use tax in New York City, so that's a lot of revenue for the city.
So Kuzlowski's art purchase got caught up in that, just unrelated and coincidentally, and ultimately those charges were dropped, because in fact there's not even a crime to charge him with.
The time is the dealer's supposed to collect that, not the customer, but the damage was already done, because the minute he reported to the board that he was being charged with the sales tax evasion charges, the board fired him immediately over the phone, they didn't even meet with him, fired him over the phone.
I believe, fully believe, if that had happened a year earlier, they would not have fired him, they would have let it play out, they would have seen, you know, wait and see what happens, you know, it's unrelated to his, his leadership of Tyco, but they were already unhappy.
So it was the perfect excuse for them to fire him.
Now here's where something really odd came into play.
A year earlier, beginning of 2001, the Tyco board became concerned because Dennis Kuzlowski had never signed an employment contract with Tyco, he was at will, he could go whenever.
And he was being recruited by a number of companies, aggressively so, you know, he had achieved great success, Tyco had grown exponentially, you know, under his leadership of CEO, they had 40 consecutive quarters where they exceeded earnings goals.
So he's racking up quite an attractive record for himself. So in order to provide assurances to Tyco shareholders, they wanted to wanted him to sign an employment contract, just an assurance that he's going to stay on.
So in 2001, early 2001, he called, he signed what they called a retention agreement that again has a mathematical calculation of, you know, if you stay eight more years, here's the amount will pay you at the end of it.
And it was based, it would be based on his highest year of earnings, that's, that's what you plug into this calculation. And at, and at that point, his highest year of earnings, I think had been about $150 million, his, his compensation, so it's highest year of compensation.
Based on that, what was already his largest year of compensation, that payout was going to be just under a half a billion dollars. So it was this huge, you know, payout at the end of the term.
In addition, if they fired him before the end of that term, let's say, you know, three years into it, they decided they didn't want him to continue.
They still had to pay out the big golden parachute. So almost a half a billion dollars in that agreement. And again, I have the agreement, I read the agreement.
The only reason that they didn't have to pay him that huge amount of money was if he was fired for cause and for cause was very narrowly defined as he was convicted of a felony that was injurious to the company.
So they fired him because of these sales tax charges, which are not related to the company and were ultimately dropped.
So then this became an issue of compensation. You know, he believed that he was do that compensation and the board did not want to pay him that compensation.
And that's where everything just kind of exploded. They brought in an independent investigator in a very short amount of time fed evidence to the Manhattan district attorney and they were charged with these serious felonies.
I, you know, it was just a convergence of really bad timing, you know, they're unhappy. They were really unhappy about that $20 million payment companies not doing particularly well, the acquisition of that financial arm of the company was failing. They were going to have to get rid of that.
Economies doing poorly, you know, so that it was and then you've got in Ron world, calm, all the other big scandals that are rolling out here in the United States at the time. And it was a really good time to hate corporate executives, especially highly paid corporate executives.
And for an elected prosecutor like the Manhattan district attorney, it certainly would be attractive to, to prosecute some of these people who were at the time, not well liked at all.
So it's just really really bad timing. And this is where, you know, we talked about, you know, the poor record keeping and the failure to observe corporate formalities and lack of oversight by the board.
That's where this really came back to hurt Coslowski and Swartz and the general council was also charged.
You know, when you don't have clear records of what happened and who did what and what was approved and wasn't approved and and and no oversight, that's where that became a huge problem.
Because when Coslowski and Swartz needed those records, they did not exist.
